statement: A bracelet has 7 equally spaced beads on a loop: 3 are black and 4 are white. Two bracelets count as the same if one can be turned or flipped over to look exactly like the other. How many different bracelets are possible?

choices.misconception: I counted every way to choose which 3 of the 7 places are black, treating turned and flipped bracelets as different.
I counted every way to share the 4 white beads among the 3 gaps between black beads, keeping the gaps in a fixed order, so I counted turned copies again.
I allowed turning the bracelet but forgot it can also be flipped, so I counted a pattern and its mirror image separately.
I sorted the bracelets into all three blacks together, exactly two together, or none together, and missed that exactly two together can happen in two different ways.

hints: Look at the white beads sitting between the black ones.
Do not count positions; count shapes. The 3 black beads split the 4 white beads into 3 gaps. Turning or flipping only moves the gaps around, so list the possible gap sizes.
The gap sizes can be 4, 0, 0 or 3, 1, 0 or 2, 2, 0 or 2, 1, 1. Check that each set of gap sizes gives just one bracelet.

solutions.reliable: The 3 black beads cut the loop into 3 gaps, and the 4 white beads are shared among those gaps. Turning the bracelet just moves the gaps round the circle, and flipping reverses their order. With only 3 gaps, any order of three gap sizes can be turned or flipped into any other, so a bracelet is fixed by its set of gap sizes alone. The possible sets are 4, 0, 0 and 3, 1, 0 and 2, 2, 0 and 2, 1, 1, so there are 4 bracelets. The transferable idea: when arrangements count as equal up to turning and flipping, describe each one by a feature that turning and flipping cannot change, rather than by positions.
solutions.elegant: Without flips there are 5 patterns, because the gaps 3, 1, 0 and 3, 0, 1 go round the circle in opposite directions and cannot be turned into each other. A flip joins exactly that pair, leaving 4.

whyOnTest: Counting up to symmetry punishes counting positions, and the wrong choices come from forgetting turns, forgetting flips, or merging two different shapes.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
